messages.subject: Re: segments for iplots?
messages.body_plain:
Ted,

On Apr 29, 2008, at 4:41 PM, Ted wrote:

> In R, there is a plotting function called 'segments'.  I was  
> wondering if there is any possibility for the iplots package to  
> include a new similar 'isegments' function?
>
> I realize iplots has 'ilines', but my dataset is quite large and  
> using ilines appears to exhaust physical memory on my desktop.


How exactly are you using ilines? I suspect that the problem lies  
there - you could write a very simple wrapper to convert isegments to  
ilines because they are functionally equivalent - somewhat like:

isegments = function (x0, y0, x1, y1, ...) {
  n = max(c(length(x0),length(y0),length(x1),length(y1)))
  x = rep(NA_real_, n*3)
  y = rep(NA_real_, n*3)
  x[1:n*3-2]=rep(x0,length.out=n)
  x[1:n*3-1]=rep(x1,length.out=n)
  y[1:n*3-2]=rep(y0,length.out=n)
  y[1:n*3-1]=rep(y1,length.out=n)
  ilines(x,y,...)
}

I could add it to iPlots, but in most cases it will be less efficient  
than using ilines, because in practice it's rather less common to have  
completely disconnected segments and thus converting the data to line  
segments instead of polylines is not advisable.

Cheers,
Simon

messages.subject: Re: JGR on windows
messages.body_plain:
On Apr 23, 2008, at 1:00 PM, Jacobs, Tim W wrote:
> Is there any way to start JGR in windows through R itself? I have an  
> application in which I use JStatCom to start R then I want to start  
> JGR. On linux, I can send several commands to R (i.e. library(JGR),  
> then JGR()). However on windows invoking JGR() must be done through  
> an outside executable?
>

In fact even the Unix version starts an outside executable. The  
difference is that the unix version creates it so it knows where it  
lives, whereas the Windows version has no idea where you put JGR.exe.  
Clearly, you can use system() in R to run JGR.exe if you tell it where  
you installed it.

Cheers,
Simon

What you think should happen is not really relevant to JGR ;). The  
JGR() function is just a way to create the JGR start script and all  
regular R startup rules apply (see R documentation).


> 2. If JGR is started with its script from outside R, I think that it  
> should not load any workspace by default, rather wait until the user  
> sets the working directory and then prompt for reading .RData

you think ;). I know a lot of users that would find that behavior very  
annoying to say the least.

Sure, the source code is freely available. But seriously, what you  
propose are not changes that make sense to me, so although technically  
possible, you'd have to convince quite a few people to warranty such  
options (because they change the behavior that many are happy with).  
In fact both have more to do with you using JGR a certain way - it's  
trivial to save/load the workspace if you want it transferred from the  
R session to JGR and it is equally trivial to just load the workspace  
after you changed the working directory if you desire to do so, so I  
really see no point here.

This seems (along with the issue of not having iplots loaded) as one

> and then start JGR() from within R, should not the default directory  
> be the one from which I started R?

JGR() is just an alias for starting the JGR script, so it will behave  
exactly as R - i.e. the workspace is restored from the directory you  
started it in. I'm not sure what you mean by "default directory" but  
the working directory is set according to your preferences. If you  
don't want the directory to be changed, use ".".

I agree that we could have some discussion about the startup - it  
would be nice to have consistent interpretation of the settings, e.g.  
to use the working directory preference for the workspace as well. It  
may be worth changing.

back-end, far more so than paining points. It is irrelevant whether  
you use segments or lines, the graphical representation is the same  
and that is where all the time is spent. therefore I have no clue why  
you are so concerned about segments. In addition, the speed depends  
heavily on the OS, aliasing settings and the opacity (no antialiasing,  
fully opaque lines are by far the fastest to draw).

First I hope you realize that the above is inherently unsafe and won't  
work properly unless you're willing to escape the filename. Note that  
you are sending the file name to the R parser, so for example
String file="c:\\foo\\dir";
eval("... file=\""+file+"\"");
will result in
c:foodir
and a few warnings in R. To avoid the quoting hell I'd suggest  
something like
assign("name",file);
eval("...file=name..");

I'm a bit surprised at the space issue - if that's true, then you have  
to use short names and that would be specific to Windows, but given  
the problems above I'm not sure it's true.

As for the umlauts, that is probably a encoding issue. Java uses UTF-8  
to encode strings, so you have to use UTF-8 locale (which you are not  
according to the sessionInfo below). If you are not then you have to  
convert the strings to the encoding you're using, e.g. using iconv().

Rserve passes all strings unmodified from the client, so currently it  
is the client's responsibility to take care of the encoding and any  
necessary conversions. However, given that AFAICS the only platform  
where this is an issue is Windows (reportedly it doesn't have a UTF-8  
locale) and Windows is quite useless for Rserve anyway, I'm not sure  
it's worth changing.

Simon

>
> What's the best approach to accomplish this using rJava/JRI?
>
> Currently I use rJava to call Java from R. That works well (it's not  
> very solid with respect to exceptions, but, hey, you can't have  
> everything!)
>

Can you, please, be specific about the last point? .jcheck()  
or .jgetEx()/.jclear() should provide all you need for Java exception  
handling (I hope) ...


> Can I just use JRI in the Java code called using rJava?

Yes, although you're entering the realm of danger. I a non-JRI R it is  
as simple as
.jengine(TRUE)
(see ?.jengine for details)


> If the answer is yes should I:
>
> - Create the R engine in R (using rJava and the constructor public  
> Rengine()) and pass it through to the Java code
> - Create the R engine in my Java code - in this case should I use  
> the public Rengine(String[] args, boolean runMainLoop,  
> RMainLoopCallbacks initialCallbacks) constructor? That would create  
> a new R instance instead of reusing the one I have. Could I use the  
> public Rengine() in this context?
>

Neither - use .jengine(). The reason is that R is already running so  
you cannot call the Rengine constructor. Instead, rJava allows you to  
get a Rengine instance for the current R process. Clearly, you cannot  
set any callbacks, because the R has already been setup.

There is one rather obscure (and hidden) function that may be useful  
for complex R->Java->R interactions: rJava:::.r2j which converts an R  
object into REXP Java object which can be returned back to the Rengine  
(yes, it sounds complicated, don't worry about it until you realize  
you need it :P).


> Is this kind of architectural solution recommended at all?
>

Depending on your OS and Java it may or may not be safe. Some OSes  
require different libraries for multi-threaded applications and since  
R was started first, it will be using single-threaded libraries. Also  
the synchronization of R and Java can be an issue if you are dealing  
with an asynchronous GUI and/or OS where threads loops can deadlock on  
UI. It is quite a delicate issue, your mileage will vary depending on  
the use etc. If it's just some computation, you should be safe, but  
anything involving UI may be dangerous.

In general you are safer using JRI, because that will run Java first  
which will setup everything for multi-threaded processing (R is run on  
a separate thread) and take care of al the synchronization. The back  
side is that JRI takes more to setup the application correctly as it  
will have to mimic R start script if you want the same environment.  
Again, it depends on what you want to do - and if JGR is an option,  
then you get it all for free since it uses JRI to run R.

Cheers,
Simon

> I have a question about the recommended architecture of an
> application in the following situation:
>
> An R program drives the overall task. The R program calls a number
> of Java functions to accomplish its goals, as it happens some of
> those function will have to call R to do their job.
>
> What's the best approach to accomplish this using rJava/JRI?
>
> Currently I use rJava to call Java from R. That works well (it's not
> very solid with respect to exceptions, but, hey, you can't have
> everything!)
>

Can you, please, be specific about the last point? .jcheck()
or .jgetEx()/.jclear() should provide all you need for Java exception
handling (I hope) ...


> Can I just use JRI in the Java code called using rJava?

Yes, although you're entering the realm of danger. I a non-JRI R it is
as simple as
.jengine(TRUE)
(see ?.jengine for details)


> If the answer is yes should I:
>
> - Create the R engine in R (using rJava and the constructor public
> Rengine()) and pass it through to the Java code
> - Create the R engine in my Java code - in this case should I use
> the public Rengine(String[] args, boolean runMainLoop,
> RMainLoopCallbacks initialCallbacks) constructor? That would create
> a new R instance instead of reusing the one I have. Could I use the
> public Rengine() in this context?
>

Neither - use .jengine(). The reason is that R is already running so
you cannot call the Rengine constructor. Instead, rJava allows you to
get a Rengine instance for the current R process. Clearly, you cannot
set any callbacks, because the R has already been setup.

There is one rather obscure (and hidden) function that may be useful
for complex R->Java->R interactions: rJava:::.r2j which converts an R
object into REXP Java object which can be returned back to the Rengine
(yes, it sounds complicated, don't worry about it until you realize
you need it :P).


> Is this kind of architectural solution recommended at all?
>

Depending on your OS and Java it may or may not be safe. Some OSes
require different libraries for multi-threaded applications and since
R was started first, it will be using single-threaded libraries. Also
the synchronization of R and Java can be an issue if you are dealing
with an asynchronous GUI and/or OS where threads loops can deadlock on
UI. It is quite a delicate issue, your mileage will vary depending on
the use etc. If it's just some computation, you should be safe, but
anything involving UI may be dangerous.

In general you are safer using JRI, because that will run Java first
which will setup everything for multi-threaded processing (R is run on
a separate thread) and take care of al the synchronization. The back
side is that JRI takes more to setup the application correctly as it
will have to mimic R start script if you want the same environment.
Again, it depends on what you want to do - and if JGR is an option,
then you get it all for free since it uses JRI to run R.

Cheers,
Simon

Hi all, 

For those interested in Rserve, I sent Simon Urbanek a question about retrieving specific error message in R using Rserve which he answered right away.  

As I understand from Simon, it is better to send these questions to this mailing list, so others can also discuss it and/ or profit from the answers. So I post our email conversation here as well.

Best regards,

Cor

-----Original Message-----
From: Simon Urbanek [mailto:Simon.Urbanek at r-project.org]
Sent: Thu 29-5-2008 17:20
To: Cor Lieftink
Cc: SCREENSAVER-DEV at LISTSERV.MED.HARVARD.EDU
Subject: Re: Question regarding Rserve, I hope you have the time to answer.
 
Cor,

On May 29, 2008, at 4:27 AM, <c.lieftink at nki.nl> <c.lieftink at nki.nl>  
wrote:

> Thank you for Rserve. In collaboration between Harvard Medical  
> School (Boston), Institute of Molecular Cell Biology (Singapore) and  
> the Netherlands Cancer Institute we use Rserve to integrate R  
> applications into a Java build webapplication called Screensaver  
> (1). We are currently integrating the first R application, called  
> cellHTS2 (2).
>
> I have the following question, I hope you find the time to answer:
> What is the best way to retrieve the specific error message in R  
> using Rserve? In case of a RserveException the only information I  
> get is "voidEval failed, request status: error code: 127". The  
> underlying error in R can however can be very different, like  
> "object not found" or a very specific error generated by the  
> cellHTS2-package using the stop-function. For now I solved the  
> problem by using the R function try (3) , which returns the exact  
> error message, but maybe I overlooked a way to get it from Rserve.
>

The short answer is you're going in the right direction.

The long answer is you have to distinguish between Rserve errors  
(communication errors, parser errors etc.) and R-side errors/ 
exceptions at evaluation time. The former are signaled by  
RserveException, the latter are not handled by Rserve directly - it's  
the user's responsibility to deal with them at R level, because that  
is where all the tools for their handling are (try, tryCatch, setting  
handlers etc.).

Although it would be possible to automatically wrap all expressions in  
try({ ... }), it would induce (unexpected) side-effects and thus I  
opted to not do that. In addition, it is trivial to add that feature  
to your application.

As for a simple error handling code, you example below is a bit  
dangerous, because it relies on the exact string value. A safer, more  
general version would be something like:

public class RException extends Exception { public RException(String  
msg) { super("R error: \""+msg+"\""); } }

static REXP safeEval(RConnection c, String s) throws RserveException,  
RException, REXPMismatchException {
   REXP r  = c.eval("try({" + s + "}, silent=TRUE)");
   if (r.inherits("try-error")) throw new RException(r.asString());
   return r;
}

Now that we are talking about it, maybe it could be added to the API  
as an alternative to eval for those that don't care that the  
expression is slightly modified.

Cheers,
Simon

PS: Please indicate whether it's ok to post this in the Rserve mailing  
list (or you may want to post a summary of the above if you wish) so  
that other people benefit from such discussions as well. Also that is  
the preferred way of asking for help unless there are privacy concerns.

Well, RConsoleOutputStream is not a subclass of PrintStream so the  
above won't work (the cast is invalid). As the documentation for  
RConsoleOutputStream says, you should be using something more like

.jcall("java/lang/System","V","setOut",.jnew("java/io/ 
PrintStream",.jcast(routput,"java/io/OutputStream")))

Cheers,
Simon

PS: You're entering quite dangerous ground there, I hope you're using  
JRI controlled R otherwise things are likely to blow up...
